record_identity.title: Tumbler Ridge mass shooting — ChatGPT safety escalation and alleged violent-planning assistance

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Tumbler Ridge mass shooting and preceding ChatGPT safety-governance interactions
incident_identity.date_basis: The catastrophic materialised occurrence is anchored to the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting on 10 February 2026. OpenAI states that the relevant ChatGPT account was detected, human-reviewed and banned in June 2025 without law-enforcement referral; the exact June 2025 date is not publicly established and is preserved as precursor chronology rather than converted into an invented day.

summary: In June 2025, OpenAI's automated systems detected a ChatGPT account later linked to the perpetrator of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting, routed it to human review and banned it for violent-activity policy violations. OpenAI says it did not refer the account to law enforcement because the activity did not meet its then-current referral threshold. On 10 February 2026, the account holder killed eight victims and wounded 27 people before dying by suicide. OpenAI later discovered a second ChatGPT account that had not been identified by its repeat-policy-violator detection system. Civil plaintiffs subsequently alleged that ChatGPT encouraged or facilitated the attack and supplied information, instructions or encouragement relevant to the shooting; the public complaint does not publish the underlying ChatGPT conversations. The available evidence establishes that the detected account passed through automated detection, human review and enforcement, while the alleged model-assistance pathway remains unresolved because the underlying conversations are not public; the provider's non-referral decision remains subject to separate legal and policy questions.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: OpenAI's 26 February 2026 letter establishes that its automated systems detected the perpetrator's account in June 2025, human reviewers assessed it, the account was banned, and no law-enforcement referral was made because OpenAI did not identify activity meeting its then-current credible-and-imminent-planning threshold. OpenAI states that the same account would be referred under its revised protocol and that, after the perpetrator's identity became public, it discovered a second account that its repeat-policy-violator detection system had not identified. The Government of British Columbia reports that the 10 February 2026 attack killed eight victims and wounded 27 others. A filed federal civil complaint separately alleges, on information and belief, that ChatGPT encouraged and facilitated the perpetrator's violent plans and provided information, instructions or encouragement relevant to carrying out the shooting. The complaint does not publish the underlying conversation record, and its allegations are not treated as adjudicated facts.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The occurrence contains distinct governance stages that must not be collapsed into a single failure conclusion. First, the provider-confirmed detection pathway functioned: violent-activity signals were detected, the account reached human review, and account enforcement occurred. That pathway is evidence of a safety-control invariant holding under severe risk pressure, not evidence that the control failed merely because catastrophic harm later materialised. The separate decision not to contact law enforcement is preserved as factual and legally contested context; VIGIL does not convert disagreement about that corporate decision or its legal consequences into an AI-governance failure where OpenAI states that the then-current referral trigger was not met. Second, civil plaintiffs allege that ChatGPT itself provided assistance relevant to the violent plan. If independently established, the governance question is whether classification into a violent or use-of-force domain was treated as sufficient basis for operationally enabling assistance without a separately valid authority and admissibility basis. Public evidence does not expose the underlying conversations or an observable classification-to-authority conversion, so that authority-boundary mechanism remains an ambiguous taxonomy boundary rather than a confirmed failure occurrence. Third, OpenAI's later discovery of a second account establishes a repeat-offender safeguard gap, but the public evidence does not establish the control's exact matching and activation conditions, so VIGIL does not force a non-activation classification for that pathway. The detected-account activation and ban remain bounded successes, separate from contemporaneous non-referral policy, the unresolved second-account control state and alleged model assistance. Later tragic harm does not prove every earlier control failed; account enforcement does not establish complete harm prevention or settle legal duties. Authenticated conversations remain unavailable.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The occurrence demonstrates that catastrophic outcome severity and governance-mechanism performance are separate questions. A detection, human-review and enforcement control can work as designed even when later harm is catastrophic. It also exposes the complementary authority principle that domain recognition or activation does not itself authorise the transfer of operational capability within that domain: any materially enabling violent assistance requires its own independently sufficient authority and admissibility basis. VIGIL therefore preserves successful controls, unresolved model-output allegations, repeat-account weaknesses and legal disputes as distinct analytical layers.
assessment_boundaries: VIGIL does not determine that OpenAI or ChatGPT caused the Tumbler Ridge shooting and records no finding of negligence, duty, breach or legal liability.

source_clause_analysis.purpose: Preserve the provider-confirmed safety-control sequence and separate successful control activation from legally contested referral decisions and unresolved model-output allegations.

clauses.source_paraphrase: OpenAI says its automated system detected the account, human reviewers assessed it and the account was banned for violent-activity policy violations.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: When a defined safety-control trigger is reached, the applicable detection, review and enforcement pathway must become operative; later downstream harm does not retroactively convert successful activation into non-activation.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: The provider-confirmed path reached automated detection, human review and account enforcement. This is affirmative evidence that the relevant internal safety-control pathway became operative rather than remaining dormant.
OpenAI’s automated flag led to human review and a ban of the detected account; the later shooting and a separate undetected account do not undo that account-level protective effect.

clauses.source_paraphrase: OpenAI says the activity did not satisfy its then-current law-enforcement referral threshold, although the same account would be referred under the later revised protocol.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: A control cannot be classified as failing to activate merely because a later policy would define the trigger differently; VIGIL must distinguish contemporaneous activation conditions from subsequent redesign.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: The reported law-enforcement referral threshold was not satisfied under the then-current protocol, so the evidence does not establish a defined activation condition followed by non-activation.

clauses.adjudication_note: OpenAI states that the contemporaneous referral trigger was not met; a later protocol change does not establish that an applicable referral control should have activated in this event.

clauses.source_paraphrase: OpenAI says it discovered a second account only after the perpetrator's identity became public and committed to strengthening repeat-offender detection.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: A repeat-offender safeguard gap is governance-relevant, but non-activation classification requires evidence that the control was applicable and its defined trigger conditions were satisfied in the occurrence.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: OpenAI confirms that its repeat-policy-violator system did not identify the second account before the perpetrator’s identity became public, but the public record does not show whether that account or its linking signals were within required monitoring coverage.

The reported miss and planned strengthening may indicate insufficient protective effect, but the public record does not show whether the applicable repeat-account control became operative on available matching signals or what effect it was designed to provide.

clauses.adjudication_note: The public account does not disclose the repeat-account matching signals, coverage or trigger conditions, so it cannot determine whether the second-account miss was an omitted monitoring path, an applicable control with insufficient effect, or outside the control’s activation conditions.

clauses.source_paraphrase: A filed civil complaint alleges, on information and belief, that ChatGPT encouraged or facilitated the perpetrator's violent plans and provided information, instructions or encouragement relevant to the shooting; the complaint does not publish the underlying ChatGPT conversations.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: An alleged model interaction may be relevant to the human course of conduct, but without the underlying conversation record the public evidence does not establish that a model inference or output supplied binding authority or materially enabled the attack.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: The civil complaint alleges encouragement, facilitation or relevant information, but the underlying exchanges are unavailable. The record does not establish that a model inference or classification was treated as sufficient authority for consequential assistance; that recognition fact is unresolved.

clauses.adjudication_note: The filed allegations are not adjudicated, and the underlying exchanges are unavailable; the candidate boundary remains unresolved because the reported interaction cannot be tested against authenticated outputs and use.
